analysis.one_liner: Exempts banks from key mortgage lending rules for loans they keep on their own books.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2016 with zero cosponsors, died in the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Truth in Lending Act so that banks and credit unions that keep a mortgage loan on their own balance sheets cannot be sued for failing to follow the 'ability-to-repay' and qualified-mortgage rules, and regulators would have to treat those loans as qualified mortgages anyway. Loan officers and brokers would also be shielded from 'steering' lawsuits when the bank plans to hold the loan, and the bill explicitly allows balloon-payment loans to qualify for this protection. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never considered before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions that hold mortgages on their own books would gain a shield from lawsuits over failing to verify a borrower's ability to repay, to limit points and fees, and to meet other qualified-mortgage requirements. Mortgage originators would gain protection from steering suits in those cases. Some borrowers who cannot meet qualified-mortgage standards might find more credit available, since banks could lend outside those rules without legal exposure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and credit unions holding mortgages

how_it_helps.text: Creates a 'safe harbor' so depository institutions cannot be sued for failing to comply with the ability-to-repay rule, points-and-fees limits, and other qualified-mortgage requirements, as long as they have held the loan on their balance sheet since it was made.
Requires banking regulators to treat a portfolio-held loan as a qualified mortgage, bypassing those rules for supervisory purposes as well.
Shields mortgage originators from steering lawsuits when the bank intends to hold the loan for its life and tells the borrower so.
Includes a rule of construction so that balloon-payment loans can qualify for the safe harbor even though they do not meet the qualified-mortgage criteria for such loans.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers who receive these portfolio loans would lose the right to sue if a bank lends them money they cannot afford or loads the loan with fees, and the protections against risky balloon-payment loans would be loosened for these loans.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes borrowers' ability to sue a bank for making a residential mortgage loan the borrower could not afford, so long as the bank keeps the loan on its books.
It explicitly allows balloon-payment loans into the safe harbor regardless of the qualified-mortgage limits on them — the loan structure most associated with the pre-2008 mortgage defaults.
It requires regulators to treat these loans as qualified mortgages, extending the exemption beyond litigation to bank supervision as well.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest trade-off: a bank that keeps a loan on its own books bears the loss if the borrower defaults, so the bill's supporters argue blanket qualified-mortgage rules add compliance costs that push lenders — especially smaller banks — out of mortgage lending. But the bill removes the legal backstop that lets a borrower challenge an unaffordable loan, and its explicit carve-out for balloon-payment loans reaches back toward the riskiest lending structure of the pre-crisis era. Weighed plainly, the lawsuit shield for banks is concrete and immediate, while the credit-access benefit for borrowers is possible but unproven — and the bill never advanced far enough for those claims to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in May 2016, referred to the Banking Committee, and never moved — no markup, no vote, and the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced S. 2995 in the Senate on May 26, 2016.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The bill received no further action and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing post-2008 mortgage protections stayed in place: banks did not get the lawsuit exemption, and borrowers kept the right to challenge unaffordable loans and the qualified-mortgage safeguards unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks didn't get the lawsuit exemption

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no pattern of party support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.note: They would be immune from ability-to-repay and qualified-mortgage lawsuits for loans they hold on their own books, and could offer balloon-payment loans outside the usual limits. The catch is that the exemption only applies if they keep the loan and its default risk on their own balance sheets, so the lender still bears the loss.
They would be shielded from steering lawsuits whenever the bank says it will hold the loan, weakening the anti-steering rule meant to keep brokers from steering borrowers into worse loans.
They get no exemption, so banks holding loans on their books would gain a legal and competitive advantage over them in mortgage lending.
